lesson_title: The Folded Corner: Similarity Proves Pythagoras
hook_text: You've used a squared plus b squared since grade 8. Grade 12 finally shows you WHY it's true — with two photographs.
clip_script: Take a right-angled triangle. Fold the corner with the right angle straight down onto the longest side. That fold cuts the triangle into two smaller ones — and here's the magic: each small triangle is a photograph of the whole thing. Check it. The small one has a right angle where the fold lands, and it shares a corner with the big triangle. Two equal angles — same shape. Guaranteed. Same shape means matching ratios, and one cross-multiplication turns a ratio into a square: left leg squared equals the hypotenuse times the piece of hypotenuse underneath that leg. The right leg tells the mirror story with the other piece. Now add them. Leg squared plus leg squared equals hypotenuse times piece one, plus hypotenuse times piece two — and the two pieces together ARE the hypotenuse. So legs squared, added, equal hypotenuse squared. That is Pythagoras — not memorised, PROVED, with nothing but the idea of an enlargement. Two photographs and one addition, and the oldest theorem in school maths opens up like a folded page.
visual_style: A paper right triangle folding its corner onto the hypotenuse, the two small triangles lifting out and enlarging to overlay the original perfectly, squares blooming off the legs and merging into the square on the hypotenuse.
pacing: Slow fold, quick angle checks, a held beat as the squares merge, clean landing.
